feature.heading: INTRODUCTION
feature.string:
Generally the System of Lyman B. Smith, in his Monograph (Smith & Downs, 1977) is followed. Some of the genera, are difficult to distinguish. The genera Vriesea and Tillandsia are distinguished from each other by the presence or absence respectively of ligules on the petal- claw. Generally, Tillandsia is characterized by having narrowly triangular leaf blades, and Vriesea by having ligulate leaf blades. However, ligules on the petal-claw may vary from present to absent even within one species (two Guiana species). Moreover, there are also many Tillandsia species having ligulate leaf blades, and Vriesea species having narrowly triangular leaf blades, or even species which have both (in different varieties). This makes these two genera highly artificial, but in my view it would be premature to put Tillandsia and Vriesea in one genus, because the Tillandsia-Vriesea group is rather heterogeneous, containing ca. 750 species, and more study of (fresh) flower material is needed to distinguish more natural groups.
Mezobromelia and Guzmania are characterized by having the petals conglutinate in a petal-tube for the length of the sepals (free or shortly conglutinate in Vriesea species). Mezobromelia species, moreover, should have ligules on the petal-claw as in Vriesea. The petals of Tillandsia pleiosticha Grisebach are only shortly conglutinate, and bear ligules on the base, and this species is therefore placed in Vriesea. There are no Mezobromelia species known from the Guiana area. Guzmania sphaeroidea (Andre) Andre ex Mez is a typical Guzmania species (close to G. altsonii L.B. Smith), but the petals are barely (if at all) conglutinate, and fall apart in living material.
Under these circumstances it would be unpractical to make separate keys for Tillandsia and Vriesea (37 species). In the key to Guzmania species, the polystichously flowered Vrieseas are included. In the key to the species of Tillandsioideae, based on vegetative characters, general characteristics of the species are used, nearly always of fullgrown plants, but measures are used as far down the key as possible. It will not always be possible to key out to the species. Descriptions are made using collections of the Guianas and surroundings only (except in Vriesea capituligera, included later), but sometimes other material is used when few collections of the Guiana area were available. The total of measured collections is given, and the Guiana collections are specified within brackets (GU = Guyana, SU = Surinam, FG = French Guiana).

question.text: Ovary inferior or nearly so; fruit baccate; seed without appendage at maturi- ty; (plant often terrestrial, mostly with spinose-serrate leaves; indument almost always of obvious scales).
Ovary superior or largely so in most genera, to inferior; fruit at least partly capsular and dehiscent, or if not (Pitcairnia in part) then the seed appen- daged.
Plant usually terrestrial, mostly with spinose-serrate leaves; indument of finely to scarcely divided scales or lacking at maturity; seed-appendages entire, slightly divided or lacking.

Plant terrestrial or epiphytic, always with entire leaves; indument mostly of obvious radially symmetric scales (or produced at one side); seed- appendages always present, finely divided and forming a coma.

feature.char: Herbs, largely epiphytic, caulescent or acaulescent.
Roots often functioning only as hold-fasts and sometimes completely lacking.
Leaves rosulate, fasciculate or distributed along a stem (distichous in only one Guiana species), entire; indument of radially symmetric or at one side produced scales.
The flowers are almost always trimerous (all Guiana species), and the perianth is clearly differentiated into sepals and petals.
The petals are nearly always similar, and vary in form from linear to ovate.
Stamens are in two whorls of 3 each.
In gamopetalous corollas the filaments are more or less fused with the petals.
The ovary consists of 3 carpels, fused at the edges, superior or nearly so (except in Glomeropitcairnia, not recorded for the Guianas).
Fruits capsular, septicidal; seeds with a plumose appendage forming a coma at the base or apex or both.

feature.string: Distribution: Nearly 1000 species in 6 (7) genera, from S. Florida to Argentina; in the Guianas ca. 51 species in 4 genera.

question.text: Flowers polystichous (more than 2-ranked), at least in part (because of the reduction of the branches to one-flowered spikes); inflorescence simple or compound.
Flowers distichous (sometimes secund at anthesis); inflorescence compound or simple or one-flowered.
Sheaths very small and inconspicuous; leaf blades very narrowly triangular and not over 1.5 cm wide.
Sheaths ample; leaf blades lanceolate or more ligulate or when narrowly triangular, then often much wider.

Inflorescence compound, at the base with a few distichously 2-3-flowered spikes, reduced to 1-flowered spikes toward the apex, there the flowers appearing polystichous; floral bracts sharply carinate when dry.
Inflorescence always simple; floral bracts not carinate.
Stem often very short; leaves cinereously lepidote; floral bracts much exceeding the sepals, lower ones caudate, green to red; sepals oblong. evenly less than half connate; petals blue.

Stem well developed; leaves lustrous-green; floral bracts just exceeding the sepals, the lower ones often not more than apiculate; pink; sepals lanceolate, posterior ones highly connate; petals normally white.
Inflorescence simple, flowers in a few rows; floral bracts partly contiguous. then loosely sheathing the flower.
Inflorescence compound, with many axillary spikes; floral bracts densely imbricate and contiguous.
Spikes (slender-) ovoid; rachis hidden, but much over 3 mm long;: the upper- primary bracts much shorter than the spikes.
Flowers fasciculate; rachis to 3 mm long; the primary bracts exceeding the spikes.
Innorescence one-flowered or rarely two-flowered; plant slender and long- caulescent, up to 8 m long, growing pendent from trees in branching strands.
Inflorescence more than two-flowered; plant acaulescent.
Plant often with more than one axillar (lateral) and simple inflorescence: the scape flat and prophyllate at the base.
Plant with one apical inflorescence, that sometimes appears lateral because the offshoot starts early near the base of the scape.
Spikes typically two-flowered (often difficult to see when dry). deeolv included in the axils of the primary bracts.
Spikes more than 2-flowered, or the inflorescence simple.
Sepals more or less asymmetrically obovate, to 0.8 cm long, but often much shorter.
Sepals (relatively) narrower and not asymmetrical, over 1 cm long.
Floral bracts ca. 2 mm long and less than half as long as the internodes; primary bracts often much shorter than the peduncle of the spikes: flowers spreading, well spaced.
Floral bracts over 4 mm long, about equaling or much longer than the internodes; primary bracts slightly shorter to much longer than the peduncles; flowers spreading or contiguous.

Rachis, floral bracts and sepals densely and ferrugineously floccose; leaves long attenuately acute; inflorescence bipinnate; primary bracts half as long to exceeding the spikes; peduncle of the spikes short, naked.

Rachis, floral bracts and sepals sparsely or subdensely appressed- and minutely lepidote, not at all ferrugineously floccose; leaves rarely long attenuately acute, mostly apiculate; inflorescence bi- or tri-pinnate; primary bracts about as long as the peduncle; peduncle to 2 cm long and oro- phyllate.
Floral bracts elliptic or ovate, 1.5-3.5 cm long, about as long as the internodes, but widely spreading with the flowers and the flowers not at all secund.
Floral bracts often much exceeding the internodes, (sub-) erect and imbricate, or secund with the flowers.

Leaf blades arching, thin, ligulate, subacute or acuminate, minutely lepidote; inflorescence,bipinnate, often of many racemes; floral bracts glabrous.
Sheaths forming a compact ovoid- or elongate pseudobulb, not over 4 cm in diam.; leaf blades fleshy or rigid coriaceous.
Plant rosulate, sometimes with a cyathiform rosette, but not bulbous; leaf blades thin or coriaceous, not fleshy.
Leaf blades fleshy, subulate-involute, not over 25 cm long, minutely appressed-lepidote or densely tomentose-lepidote.
Leaf blades rigid-coriaceous, not subulate-involute, very narrowly triangular, mostly involute when dry, cinereous-lepidote.
Plant wholly very densely tomentose-lepidote; floral bracts 2-2.9 cm long
Sheaths and bracts cinereous-lepidote at least near the apex; leaf blades minutely lepidote and lustrous-green; floral bracts 1.1-1.9 cm long.

Floral bracts 1.3-1.9 cm long, about equaling the sepals, glabrous at least in lower half; sheaths contracted into the blades; leaf blades many times longer then the sheaths, mostly strongly recurved, filiform attenuate.

Sepals much exceeding the noral bracts at anthesis.
Sepals slightly, if at all, exceeding the floral bracts.

Floral bracts 3-4 times as long as the internodes, widely spreading with the flowers, but not secund, ecarinate; sepals 3-3.5 cm long
Spikes linear, (sub-)terete, 10-50 cm long and not over 1.2 cm in diam.; floral bracts over 4.5 cm long.
Spikes more or less complanate, mostly over 1.2 cm wide or the bracts far less than 4.5 cm long.
Leaf blades narrowly triangular, filiform attenuate; axis of the inflorescence elongate; floral bracts 1-1.5 times as long as the internodes. often expos- ing the rachis for most part when dry.
Leaf blades broadly ligulate, broadly rounded and triangular-acuminate;. floral bracts over 2 times as long as the internodes, slightly (if at all) exposing the rachis when dry.
Leaf blades (very) narrowly triangular, evenly tapering from the base to the apex, or triangular-ovate-lanceolate and not over 50 cm long.
Leaf blades not evenly tapering from the base to the apex, more linear (-lanceolate) or ligulate.
Leaf blades thin, mostly not over 1.5 cm wide, lustrous-green in part; inflorescence always simple.
Leaf blades (sub-)coriaceous or over 2 cm wide at the base, mostly cinereous- lepidote; inflorescence rarely simple.
Floral bracts spreading with the flowers, and not imbricate at anthesis. to 1.6 cm long.
Floral bracts imbricate at anthesis, over 2.3 cm long.
Floral bracts imbricate, but the upper ones with free apices, much exceeding the sepals, sharply conduplicate but ecarinate; scape often strongly curved downward; spike fan-like.
Floral bracts wholly contiguous with each other, just exceeding the sepals, sharply alate-carinate at the apex; scape erect; spike obovate (-lanceolate).
Leaves filiform-attenuate.
Leaves acute, not filiform at the apex.
Floral bracts not over 2 cm long; axis of the inflorescence (when comnound) elongate.
Floral bracts over 2.5 cm long; axis reduced to nearly none.
Inflorescence erect; spikes mostly over 2.5 cm wide; floral bracts 4.5-5.5 cm long, sharply carinate in upper half.
Inflorescence pendulous; spikes less than 2 cm wide; floral bracts not over 3.5 cm long, ecarinate.
Sheaths in upper part dull and often dark ferrugineously lepidote outside; sepals to 1.5 cm long, posterior ones more than half connate.
Sheaths minutely pale-brown, not ferrugineous-lepidote in upper part; sepals over 2 cm long and less connate.
Sepals not over 2.7 cm long, posterior ones less than half, but distinctly connate; sheaths about as long as the leaf blades, often dark purole-brown inside; the blade cinereous-lepidote throughout.
Sepals 3-5 cm long, free; sheaths ample, but often not very distinct and not so long as the blade; the leaf blade soon glabrescent at the uooerside.
Inflorescence bi- or tri-pinnate.
Inflorescence simple.
Axis sometimes evident, but barely visible because of erect primary bracts and spikes; primary bracts large, slightly shorter than the soikes.
Axis visible for most of its length; primary bracts hardly exceeding the sterile part of the branches.
Floral bracts rigid-coriaceous, often strongly incurved toward the apex. 3-5.5 cm long, about equaling the sepals.
Floral bracts not strongly incurved, not over 2.8 cm long.

Floral bracts mostly secund with the flowers at anthesis, 3-4 cm long; scape slender (4-7 mm in diam.); leaves triangular-subacute, often reddish.

feature.string:
Note: Vriesea differs from Tillandsia by bearing 2 ligules at the base of the petal-claw. These ligules are often reduced and very difficult to find, even present or absent within one species (at least in 2 species recorded for the Guianas: Vriesea incurva and Vriesea duidae). This makes the distinction of Vriesea highly artificial, but it is not recommended to put Vriesea simply into synonymy of Tillandsia. More study of the flowers is needed to distinguish more natural groups (genera) within the Tillandsia-Vriesea complex.
KEY: For practical reasons, pointed out before, the species of Vriesea and Tillandsia are combined in one key (see under Tillandsia).

feature.string: Culture and use: Commercially grown in great numbers for a long period of time; in cultivation usually only select forms (cultivars) are found, known as the "Flaming Sword"; easily grown in window and greenhouse at a bright (not sunny) location; demands watering between the sheaths.

Floral bracts about 6 times as long as the internodes.

feature.char: Plant acaulescent, flowering ca. 80 cm long, with a dense, 40-60 cm tall rosette.
Capsule (slenderly) ellipsoid, 2.5-3.5 cm long, slightly exceeding the bracts, rounded, then abruptly short-beaked.
